hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Graeme Downie
hansard.text: My hon. Friend is absolutely correct. Again, as I discussed when talking about the need for a joined-up approach across the United Kingdom, and she made this point powerfully in her speech and through interventions, we must wherever possible work across multilateral organisations, such as UNESCO, to help spread this work because we do not want to solve the problem here but have it moved elsewhere. Fundamentally, we have a role as a leading country in free speech and in guaranteeing access to justice, and we must not just protect that here, but advocate and push for it in other forums, too. As has been discussed, this Bill has cross-party support and support across Administrations, including in Scotland. The right hon. Member for Maldon mentioned in his introductory speech that the Bill was stopped by a general election, which I think he described as catastrophic. I cannot quite remember the exact word that he used, but that Bill had been brought forward by my former hon. Friend, Wayne David, when he was the Member for Caerphilly. I do not think Wayne would mind me saying that it was perhaps worth losing the Bill to win the election, knowing that someone experienced and with a track record on these issues would bring the legislation forward again, ensuring that we could none the less win an election and then his Bill would ultimately be passed. He is probably sitting somewhere thinking that he got everything he could possibly want. Since the election, this Bill has been brought back, rewritten and brought back again. That is how we have ended up with the Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill, with a twin version introduced in the other piece by Baroness Stowell. To be honest, it is starting to feel like a film franchise. We have now had the origi

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Alex Sobel (Leeds Central and Headingley) (Lab/Co-op)
hansard.text: I thank the right hon. Member for Maldon (Sir John Whittingdale) not just for this Bill, but for his many years of work in this area for citizens of the UK and everybody in the future who will not be affected by this pernicious practice if we are successful today. I also thank many of my hon. Friends who have already contributed and spoke in the SLAPPs debate that I led not long ago, which in many ways was a precursor to today's legislation. I hope that it proved useful in helping to refine the Bill before us. Strategic lawsuits against public participation are no more than the wealthy and powerful abusing the British legal system in order to silence critics, victims and people speaking up for the public interest, including so many ordinary people, as we just heard from my hon. Friend the Member for Penrith and Solway (Markus Campbell-Savours). Unfortunately, the UK has become a hotbed of SLAPPs by being identified as the leading source of them, with more than nearly all EU countries and the United States combined. SLAPPs hold very little legal merit but are so debilitating financially, often to serve the purpose of the claimant and silence the target into submission. We must have effective and watertight anti-SLAPP legislation. We need policy that can withstand and endure the meticulous and solvent legal forces of the rich and powerful. Recent months in the UK have seen the immense bravery of people speaking up at the cost of their own privacy to stand strong in the public interest. Our legal system must be able to weather that and protect the bravest people and not inadvertently cripple them into silence. We justifiably have a worldwide reputation for our legal system, the independence of our judiciary and its robustness, but unfortunately that is being critically und

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Alicia Kearns (Rutland and Stamford) (Con)
hansard.text: I wish to praise my right hon. Friend the Member for Maldon (Sir John Whittingdale) for introducing the Bill, not least because he has spent the past two weeks fighting to save the most famous product in his constituency. I hope that he has every success in doing so. I want to begin with two young women. Each of them went online to warn other women, and each of them was sent a letter by a lawyer. The first posted questions on Instagram about Enough, a company selling self-swab rape kits to women and girls. In May, I told this House what happened next. A letter signed by the company's founders accused her of scaremongering. It threatened an injunction, damages for defamation and legal costs. A further message told her to reflect on what this might mean for her future employment opportunities—her career, her reputation, her entire future. They told her it would be in ruin. The law firm then sent a cease and desist. Rape support charities, shamefully, received the same letters. Let that sink in: Enough targeted not just individual women and survivors, but the very charities that speak up on sexual violence, that campaign to protect women and to which women go in their darkest hours. The money donated to support women and children had to be spent on responding to predatory legal letters. Was the young girl wrong to ask questions online? Was she wrong to ring the alarm bell about the company's language and behaviour towards young women? Well, the Advertising Standards Authority does not think so. It found that Enough had misled the public about whether its kits could be used in court, about the number of rapes that take place in our country and in claiming that women are more likely to be raped than to get cancer—categorically untrue. The police have warned against the kits,

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Markus Campbell-Savours
hansard.text: I welcome the intervention; I absolutely want to work together with everybody. It is interesting that there is no one sitting on the Lib Dem and Reform Benches for this debate. That is disappointing, but part of me wonders whether many of the victims, like the constituent I will talk about in my speech, simply do not come forward and say what happened to them. The nature of SLAPPs means that many people probably just disappear into silence. The person at the centre of my story—I am sorry if hon. Members have heard his story before—is a gentleman by the name of Jeff Thomson. Jeff is a retired resident of Penrith, who started campaigning around the long-standing odour problem known locally as the “Penrith pong”. In 2022, he established a Facebook group called Fresh AIR for Penrith, where residents could share information, discuss their experiences and exchange advice on reporting concerns to the relevant authorities. In February 2023, following comments made on that forum regarding the town's meat rendering plant, which has for many years been considered the source of the smell, Jeff received legal correspondence alleging defamation. Having read the material in question, and even with no legal background, I saw a clear attempt to gag Jeff, and I was shocked that the legal firm, which I will not name, would pursue the matter. What followed was more than three years of uncertainty before the claim was ultimately discontinued in June this year. Unlike many people subjected to this kind of pressure, Jeff can now speak openly about what he experienced. He remains grateful for the support he received from the UK Anti-SLAPP Coalition, Index on Censorship, and Reynolds Porter Chamberlain LLP. What struck me most about the case was the imbalance between the parties. On one side st

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Graeme Downie
hansard.text: We have heard examples from other Members about local campaigners who have been affected by this issue as a result of Facebook posts and other posts on social media. Does my hon. Friend agree that not only is the individual threatened, but word then spreads throughout the community that a person has been threatened with legal action, resulting in a much broader impact? The threat is therefore actually much wider, and can involve everyone in the campaign. A SLAPP does not just affect one person; it can spread like a virus throughout a whole community very quickly and discourage people from taking part in that campaign, and in future ones.

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Alex Sobel
hansard.text: My hon. Friend is absolutely right. For people who do not have a lot of money, this is about the financial threat to them—the threat to their ability to access or transact their own money in banks, to their houses, if they own them, and to their wider family. That is one major way that SLAPPs are used to silence people in this country. The key indicators that the letter of claim may constitute a SLAPP are as follows. The letters are written in an oppressive fashion to a litigant in person whom Taylor Hampton should know was unlikely to have good knowledge of the English legal system. The letters use inappropriate headings—for instance, “STRICTLY PRIVATE AND CONFIDENTIAL—NOT FOR PUBLICATION OR ONWARD DISSEMINATION”. The letters seek an apology on the SJS website—an organisation that has no connection to the claim and a remedy to which Premier bank cannot possibly be entitled. The letter of claim seeks “very substantial” damages in circumstances where such damages are fanciful, not least because there was no evidence that the Horn Observer articles were authored by Mumin, and it will have been obvious to Premier bank that the vast majority of the readership of the articles and Mumin's social media accounts were based in Somalia, not here. Abdalle's tweets and Facebook posts are clearly in the public interest, given the prior conduct of the Somali state towards Abdalle, reinforced by the alleged connection between Premier bank and the Somali state through the President's alleged stake in the bank, and the communications from the Minister and bank representative. Fundamentally, Taylor Hampton sent the letter of claim to a refugee with an extensive history of persecution by the state in which Premier bank is incorporated, in circumstances where there is considerable reason t

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Adam Thompson
hansard.text: My hon. Friend is being very generous with his time. I was watching a YouTube video last night by a creator called JimmyTheGiant, who creates some really interesting content, and he touched on my hon. Friend's point about churches being repurposed as mosques. Actually, far more churches in the country have been repurposed as everything else under the sun—business centres, for example. I think this issue is being weaponised by a certain subsection of our political sphere. Could my hon. Friend elaborate on the many reasons why churches might be repurposed? It is certainly not for nefarious purposes.

hansard.speaker: Adam Thompson (Erewash) (Lab)
hansard.text: I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Stoke-on-Trent Central (Gareth Snell) for introducing the Bill. As he elaborated, Stoke is a world-famous location for its ceramics industry, and he is always a great advocate for his constituents and industry. He nicely segued into my speech, because he used the apex of his speech to discuss Denby pottery, which is what I would like to begin with. Just a 20-minute drive from Ilkeston and Erewash, in the constituency of my hon. Friend the Member for Amber Valley (Linsey Farnsworth), sat Denby Pottery Village, and I would like to go through some of the history. Since 1809, handcrafted ceramics, mainly tableware and kitchenware, were produced there. I was raised on Denby pottery, as my mum was a great advocate for it when I was a youngster, and it was famous for its excellent design and high quality. In the 19th century, as today, Derby was a crucial rail hub, and Denby pottery benefited enormously from close rail connections to Derby city. By the end of the century, it was a global exporter, and by the 1920s its ceramics were both collector's items and household products around the world. It only expanded from there, becoming a publicly traded company in 1970. All the while, Denby Pottery's commercial success and iconic brand were a source of local pride for Denby village and, indeed, all of us in Derbyshire, as my hon. Friend the Member for Stoke-on-Trent Central indicated. It was a great British success story and one built on hard work and carefully cultivated skill. I know from my constituents—particularly those in Ilkeston—that, as well as a local industry, Denby Pottery Village was a great day, for visiting and doing some shopping. Most importantly, the village provided great local jobs. It was work in the arts sector, which I k

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Alicia Kearns
hansard.text: The hon. Lady is absolutely right. We should support international efforts around the world, not least because we know many people often come to our courts to litigate through them because we are so trusted. We should also support such efforts so that SLAPPs are not used in this way, particularly in the Commonwealth but also more broadly, because if SLAPPs are being abused in the way they are in this country, imagine the way they are in other countries where journalism and civil society are not as strong as they are here and where both those vital pillars of our democracy are, frankly, often under attack. I want to touch on two cases that my right hon. Friend the Member for Maldon also touched on. The first is Eliot Higgins, a good friend who started out as a blogger teaching himself to check footage from Syria against satellite images. He went on to form Bellingcat, which has produced products that Governments around the world rely on. He showed that the Assad regime was using cluster munitions and chemical weapons against its own people. We failed to act as a House, but at least he exposed it. It traced the missile launcher that shot down MH17, killing 298 people to Russia's 53rd Anti-Aircraft Missile Brigade. That was before the international investigators reached the same finding. He uncovered the evidence that Russian military intelligence was behind the Novichok attack in Salisbury and identified the specific FSB team that poisoned Alexei Navalny. It turned the same skills on people who exploit children and women around the world, helping Europol to trace images of child sexual abuse and exposing the most notorious deepfake pornography site until it was shut down for good. Elliot and Christo are our modern-day heroes, and they have had enormous costs imposed on th

hansard.speaker: Gareth Snell
hansard.text: It is as though the hon. Gentleman has seen the next bullet point in my very scrappy notes. I do not know what the Minister will say in his speech—that is obviously for him—but I suspect that he has had a note to say that trading standards cannot enforce the Bill. Well, we pass many laws in this place and expect the enforcement agencies to enforce them, not least the changes that we have made to vaping laws. That is a huge piece of work that we expect trading standards to carry out. The Minister may have been told by an official—if it was the same official who spoke to me—that consumers do not want the Bill and quite like the idea that they can buy a cheap piece of crockery or ceramics. It is all about the consumer and the market. It might well be that consumers do not care—but I do. My constituents who work at Dunoon, Duchess, Steelite and Churchill care, because it is their job. I can always tell whether somebody is from Stoke-on-Trent, because wherever they happen to be, they will pick up the plate they are eating off, turn it over and look at the bottom. It is a running joke in the Tea Room—people see me do it and they think I am being daft, but I am checking. It is also a moment of pride. There is something called the “turnover club”—you can become a member of it, Madam Deputy Speaker; anyone can become a member—of people who check where their crockery has been made. Members of this House have been very helpful in that regard; everyone here was sent a QR code, which they could use to tell me where they found crockery made in Stoke-on-Trent, and many Members sent me examples from their own constituencies where British-made ceramics were being used. This proposal may not be what consumers as a whole want—but I bet that most consumers do not realise that, when they wa

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Dame Nia Griffith
hansard.text: I believe that my hon. Friend very recently had a debate on exactly the subject of what hybrid warfare is costing the UK Government. He is absolutely right; we still have not found the right mechanisms with which to refute and deal with the absolute onslaught of hybrid attacks we are suffering. The worry for me is that, without challenging them, we will embolden our enemies to go further and further. We have seen them pushing out the boat in all sorts of different directions and types of attacks, both physical and intellectual, such as on the internet, in brainwashing, in cyber-attacks and in the incursions into NATO territory that we have seen. That very much worries me. There is an imperative here from a national security perspective as well as the personal perspective that we have heard about. There is also an imperative in the principle that we should have freedom of speech, and it should not depend on people's ability to pay enormous, ridiculous sums to silence other people. That should not dictate who has the opportunity to speak up. I very much commend this Bill to the House, and I wish the right hon. Member for Maldon absolutely every success in seeing it through.

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Dame Nia Griffith
hansard.text: My hon. Friend mentions something that we all agree with. We have had a very constructive debate, but those who oppose us will criticise us. When we leave this place and look at social media, we will see that other people have very different views, as he has just mentioned. Will he confirm that this Bill is about the abusive use of legislation and does not prevent the legitimate use of legislation? There are still protections in place for taking forward what is reasonable and legitimate, but this Bill tackles the abusive use of a legal tool to persecute, pursue and harass people.

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Graeme Downie
hansard.text: My hon. Friend is absolutely right. The House will be delighted to know that I will shortly bring my remarks to a close. As I mentioned earlier, it is important that we talk about what happens across different parts of the UK and that they are joined up. For example, we have seen it suggested that Scottish defamation law is quite different from what we see in England. That has been used from the Spycatcher affair right through to the Ryan Giggs super-injunction. Scottish papers could cover those stories in a way that was not allowed in England. Indeed, there were suggestions on social media just last week that Scottish newspapers could have covered the David Walliams story, as they were not covered by the injunction. The reason why the newspapers did not do that is that they behaved professionally and said, “We do not have the evidence, so we are not going to publish this, because we are not the holders of the evidence.” That was to their great credit. However, the anti-SLAPP research hub at Aberdeen University has warned that, without legislation, Scotland risks becoming a haven for this kind of work. That is why I am very keen that the Minister engages on that issue. A former Member of this House, Roger Mullin, who was the Member for Kirkcaldy and Cowdenbeath—just next door to my constituency—took a petition on this issue to Holyrood in 2022. I do not agree with Roger on a great deal, but he was absolutely right on this matter, and Ministers have committed to legislate at the next opportunity. We have heard from across the House that SLAPPs are a real problem, and they are getting worse. They are used by wealthy people against those with far less, by hostile states and by businesses to keep their friends out of the papers. However, very often the threat of being sued

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Graeme Downie
hansard.text: I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Erewash (Adam Thompson) for his intervention, if for no other reason than it gives me an opportunity to say the word “Erewash” again. I remember an instance in this House, quite soon after the election, when he and I enjoyed saying the word “Erewash”. I think we managed to say it 10 or 15 times in very short order, perhaps to be mischievous towards our very talented and expert colleagues in Hansard , who were trying to write it down at the time. My hon. Friend is absolutely right. Intimidation through non-engagement and the denial of free speech is something that we need to be very careful about. Sadly, the Reform party has a record of doing that. It uses different methods to shut down voices and intimidate local communities, including by not working with journalists, which is outrageous. I will come on to that later. In my own constituency, Reform issued a statement last week that complained in some very horrible language—sadly, we have become all too used to it—about a church in the centre of Dunfermline, which was taken over by a local mosque a number of years ago. The church was declining and, sadly, had been closed for a number of years—it had essentially become derelict. The mosque took over the building and has done a fantastic job. It is community-focused and does an incredible amount of work in the local area. Last week, Reform used social media to intimidate mosque users and to decry the fact that the church has been taken over. Sadly, we see Reform using different ways to intimidate people. I am delighted to say that the local community in Dunfermline have come together and said that the mosque is a valuable part of our community and we welcome what it does. My hon. Friend the Member for Erewash is absolutely right to hig

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Graeme Downie (Dunfermline and Dollar) (Lab)
hansard.text: Friday sittings sometimes get an odd reputation in the House, but I have learned a lot in the last three hours. As I mentioned in a few interventions, I knew a little bit about the issue, but had not thought about it perhaps in the way that I should have. Debates in the House are sometimes sadly curtailed—and clipped for social media—to ensure we get through business and scrutinise the Government, so the opportunity to have a more extensive debate is welcome, especially as the issue is quite technical and complicated. Frankly, the acronym does not do it due justice, given the extent to which the issue can affect all our constituents. Whether it is private Members' Bills, ten-minute rule Bills or the various other ways that issues can be raised, I am sure that all Members appreciate the value of listening for a few hours to detailed debate in the Chamber, and feel that it would be helpful to have more time to do that. This has been a fascinating debate. My wife is a former litigation lawyer, so some of my remarks may or may not have been coloured or influenced by speaking to her over the years. There are differences between our legal systems in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, but none the less, there is commonality between some of the challenges that we face. As a United Kingdom—if the hon. Member for Strangford (Jim Shannon) were here, he would insist upon saying that it is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland—there are areas where we should work together. As has been highlighted across the Chamber, this issue is not party-political; there is cross-party support and understanding of what needs to happen. That is the same in Scotland, and I am sure it is the same in Wales and in Northern Ireland. A common approach across the different l

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Sir John Whittingdale (Maldon) (Con)
hansard.text: I beg to move, That the Bill be now read a Second time. It is a privilege to have the opportunity to introduce a private Member's Bill. I have entered the ballot every year for 34 years, but this is the first time I have had the opportunity to move a Second Reading. Like, I am sure, all those hon. Members who came out high in the ballot, many worthy causes were suggested to me that were subject to legislation. However, I decided to introduce this Bill to increase the protection for defendants against what are called strategic lawsuits against public participation, but that are actually attempts to muzzle free speech and to silence those who wish to publicise wrongdoing, as a result of journalistic investigation, as whistleblowers or sometimes as victims as well. I have a long-standing commitment and interest in media freedom. I chaired the all-party parliamentary group on media freedom, and during my times in Government, I sought to promote media freedom, both in this country and abroad. The United Kingdom's ranking in terms of media freedom is high. We are currently 18th in the world league according to Reporters sans Frontières, who produce the world press freedom index, but 18th is not good enough—we should be higher. According to the RSF analysis, one reason the UK does not score higher is the number of cases that have been brought that are plainly SLAPPs, and the fact that we do not have adequate protection against them. That is something that I hope we may put right today. I first became aware of the problem in 2010, as Chair of the Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee that produced a report on press standards, privacy and libel. Since then, there have been a number of debates, further publications and indeed some progress, with some steps being taken. Under

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Sarah Sackman
hansard.text: My hon. Friend is absolutely right. Fundamentally, our courts must be a forum for justice, never a weapon for intimidation. Whether legislating against non-disclosure agreements, supporting the legislation before us today or working in a number of other ways, this Government are determined to stop the wealthy and the powerful from using the threat of costly legal proceeding to supress legitimate scrutiny. It takes extraordinary courage to speak out against the rich, the famous and the powerful. This Bill is for the victims of abuse, whistleblowers and journalists. For those determined to expose wrongdoing, coming forward can be daunting enough. Imagine facing not only the prospect of being disbelieved but financial ruin, simply for daring to tell the truth. Recent events have brought into sharp focus how those suspected of abuse can wield their wealth and influence to intimidate their accusers, and to suppress the publication of investigations into their own behaviour. They raise a troubling question: how many stories never see the light of day because those implicated have the money and power to bury them in court proceedings? For too long, these actors and powerful organisations have used the threat of costly legal proceedings to suppress legitimate scrutiny. The cynical claims that we have heard about, known as strategic litigation against public participation—as my hon. Friend the Member for Cities of London and Westminster (Rachel Blake) said, SLAPPs is an ugly word for an ugly thing—are often the first weapon of choice for oligarchs and kleptocrats keen to keep their dirty dealings out of the headlines. However, their reach extends much further, and Members from across the House poignantly expressed the experiences of their own constituents. No area of our society

hansard.debate: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill
hansard.speaker: Sarah Sackman
hansard.text: I come back to where I started. Today is not a common occurrence, where across the House there is agreement and collaboration which I know will continue over the coming months. This is a difficult area of legislation. It is not difficult to see the abuse and not difficult to see that we need to do something about it. It is about getting the balance right, which I will come on to in a minute, between protecting freedom of expression and access to justice where people have legitimate claims. I hope that when those Members take the time to take their places, whether from the Liberal Democrats or Reform, they too will see the merit in pursuing legislation in this space. ECCTA is simply not enough, so it is clear to me that this is an area where more legislation is needed. It is why I have been happy, over the previous weeks and months, to work on the Bill with the right hon. Member for Maldon. Let us look at what the Bill, which I regard as a major step forward, will do. As I said, the Bill will protect journalists, campaigners and ordinary people from those who use wealth and their legal might to silence scrutiny. I believe that the Bill is balanced and effective. How does it achieve that balance? First, it creates a vital early dismissal mechanism. Put simply, if the court identifies that the case before it is a SLAPP—that it meets the test for an abusive claim—then it can be struck out at the first time of asking, removing the stress that comes with the delay of a long, drawn-out legal process. Courts will be able to dispose swiftly of SLAPPs that lack legal merit, where the claimant cannot show that the case is more likely than not to succeed and the public interest favours dismissal.
